identity.audience: Builders on X: developers and technical founders who ship products.

angles.brief: A clear, defensible opinion on ONE item: what it changes for people shipping products, developers or founders. The take goes in the first line, the concrete reason from the item right after. Be specific enough that someone could disagree.
Read ONE item as a business story: pricing, costs, margins, distribution, who wins and who loses, what it does to SaaS or to startups. Use the numbers from the item where they exist.
Make it worth bookmarking. From ONE item: a one-line hook, then 2-3 concrete things a builder should check, change, or try because of it, one short line each. Only specifics the item supports.
Push back on the obvious reading of ONE item, with a specific reason from the item. Firm, not snarky. Never dunk on a person or a company.
What ONE release, tool, or deal actually changes, in plain words, for someone building a real product. Lead with the consequence, not the announcement.

Read ONE item from the seat of a CS undergrad who ships side projects: what it changes for students, juniors, and interns learning to build right now (what to learn, what stops mattering, what gets more valuable). A real opinion, stated plainly. Never invent personal events, grades, offers, or internships.

Point builders at ONE item worth their time (a talk, a post, a repo, a paper) and say in one or two lines exactly why it is worth it and who it is for. Curation with a real reason, not a summary. Name it in words, no link.
ONE thing tried in this week's work and what happened. Lead with the result or the surprise, then what was tried. Only what the commits show.
ONE specific problem hit this week and exactly how it was fixed, concrete enough that another builder would bookmark it.
ONE build decision made this week, the tradeoff, and the reason, stated plainly enough that someone could argue with it.
Open with the single most useful thing learned this week, then what shipped, then what is next.
Open with the most concrete thing shipped this week, then the lesson it taught, then what is being worked on now.
A one-line hook about the week, then three short lines: something learned, something shipped, something in progress.
ONE real gotcha in the topic: the behavior that surprises people, why it happens, and the fix. Concrete enough to bookmark.
ONE common pattern in the topic and the better one, with the reason in one line. Show the actual function, flag, or syntax by name.
ONE small, little-known but long-stable feature in the topic that saves real time, and when to reach for it.
ONE idea that makes the topic click: how it actually works under the hood, in two or three plain lines.
From ONE news item: a specific question working builders can answer from their own experience, with the author's own lean stated first so it is a conversation, not a poll.
A real tradeoff inside the topic that experienced developers disagree on. State which way the author leans and why in one line, then ask what others pick and when.

A specific question a CS student who builds things would genuinely want answered by people ahead of them (about learning, shipping, or working with AI tools), anchored to ONE news item or the topic. No invented personal events.

A short, relatable observation about building software that working developers will recognize instantly (debugging, deploys, naming, estimates, side projects, docs). Dry and specific, not a joke template. One to three lines.
A short, honest observation about what coding with AI tools is actually like day to day: where it helps, where it quietly costs time. Specific, not hype and not doom.

A short observation from the seat of a CS undergrad who ships side projects: the gap between coursework and building real things, learning in public, what actually teaches you. No invented personal events, grades, offers, or internships.
One firm, defensible opinion about software development practice in one or two lines, stated plainly enough that someone will reply to disagree. Never dunk on a person or company.
